Those counting bounds are then advertised as the input to new zero-density estimates, with Halasz-Montgomery large-values machinery, Huxley-type reflection ideas, and critical-line fourth moments providing the leverage. Because the OCR damages several formulas and exponents, the trustworthy trainable object is the reduction itself and the three-case architecture, not the numerical details.

interpretations.interpretation:
Montgomery's pair-correlation framework replaces one-point zero counts by a statistic of zero differences. Assuming RH, the span defines the weighted function F_alpha(X), records its symmetry and positivity, states the proved asymptotic in a restricted range, and then presents the stronger conjectural min(1,|beta|) form.

The proved-versus-conjectural split is mathematically central. The definition itself makes zero spacing observable in a new representation, but stronger consequences like almost-all simplicity belong to the conjectural extension, not to the established range alone.

The proof does not force positivity for every shift. Instead it averages over shifts with a weight K(delta), shows that the averaged quantity has a positive main term despite the error terms, and then uses continuity to extract one concrete shift where the contribution stays positive.

That averaged positivity is immediately converted into existence. After expanding the prime integrals and bounding the diagonal and off-diagonal parts, the source concludes that there must be primes p<q in the stated ranges with q-p controlled by K^2 times the larger of two short-scale quantities.

The opening states two linked zero-control theorems near s = 1. Landau's result says that two distinct real primitive character L-functions cannot both have real zeros too close to 1, while Page's theorem says that a single real non-principal character L-function has at most one simple real zero in the dangerous interval near 1. The span also notes that Burgess's inequality sharpens that interval.

The conceptual move is a zero-repulsion principle: exceptional real zeros are constrained collectively rather than behaving as independent accidents. The author also emphasizes a method change, replacing functional-equation or complex-function arguments with a simpler real-analysis route, while the exact constants are partially obscured by OCR.

Assuming RH, the note claims an exceptional-set refinement of the prime number theorem remainder: outside a set of finite logarithmic measure, the error term improves from O(x^(1/2)log^2 x) to O(x^(1/2)(log log x)^2). The same span also gives short proofs of mean-square bounds for psi(x)-x and uses them to derive almost-all remainder estimates and a conditional normal-density statement for primes in short intervals.

The concrete move is to trade a uniform pointwise estimate for an exceptional-set formulation supported by average control. The finite logarithmic measure of the bad set is the key gain in this excerpt. Because the unit is OCR text, the interpretation stays at the prose level of the stated bounds and their relation rather than leaning on every damaged symbolic detail.

The consequences in this span come from averaging the explicit zero formula instead of reading it pointwise. Equation (8) yields one result by a splitting-up argument, while the mean-square consequence is obtained by logarithmically averaging a squared zero-sum expression and choosing a truncation parameter T=T_gamma with T tending to infinity but log T=o(log X).

The averaging step is the mechanism. Cross terms from distinct zeros are damped by the logarithmic integral, so the source can obtain a C log X mean-square law for psi(x)-x even though exact pointwise control remains much more delicate.

interpretations.interpretation:
The survey presents RH equivalences as translations made possible by the explicit-formula duality between primes and zeros. Once that bridge is accepted, prime-counting error statements and zero-set statements become different surfaces of the same claim.

This span uses that idea at the overview level. It lists the Li(x)+O(x^(1/2+epsilon)) form, the von Koch bound, and Schoenfeld's explicit inequality as equivalent prime-side formulations, without trying to reprove them. The trainable content is the equivalence map itself: error structure is preserved while the visible objects change from zeros to prime counts.

The paper proposes a spectral interpretation in which zeta zeros appear on the spectral side as an absorption spectrum: critical zeros appear directly, while noncritical zeros enter as resonances through their harmonic potential relative to the critical line. The span also reports preliminary spectral and trace-formula results on adele-class spaces, including local and finite-place trace formulas that recover the corresponding Weil explicit-formula terms, and it highlights the elimination of the auxiliary parameter delta.

The conceptual shift is from locating zeros to establishing a global trace formula whose spectral and geometric sides coincide. The source explicitly does not claim that global step is complete here: it says the global trace formula is left open and that its validity would be equivalent to RH for Groessencharakter L-functions. The excerpt is therefore an open spectral program with concrete local pieces, not a finished spectral proof.

The span extends Jensen-function methods from ordinary almost periodicity to the generalized almost periodic setting needed for 1/2 < sigma < 1. In that setting, mean motion for log zeta(s) - x on a vertical line and zero frequency in a strip are both read off from one twice differentiable convex Jensen function: its derivative gives the mean motion, and derivative differences give strip-zero frequencies.

That is a real representation gain, not just summary prose. The source turns several zero-distribution questions into calculus on a single function of sigma, and it explicitly says the enabling step is the extension beyond the sigma > 1 regime where ordinary almost periodicity already worked.

Riemann first uses an argument-principle count to estimate how many roots of xi lie in a bounded region, then reports that one indeed finds about that many real roots and says it is very probable that all roots are real. He immediately marks that stronger claim as unproved and unnecessary for his next step.

The operative move is disciplined separation of evidence and dependence. The source continues with a logarithmic product expansion over all roots alpha because that representation only needs control of root density and existence, not a proof that every root is real or an ordering of them on the line.

The source starts from the Nyman-Beurling closure criterion in a Hilbert space of Beurling functions and then makes a sharper claim about what generators are actually needed. Instead of approximating chi with the full continuum of dilations, it proposes that the natural-number subfamily already carries the whole RH criterion.

That is a genuine thinning operation on the representation. The ambient closure problem stays the same, but the generating family is compressed from all real a >= 1 to integer a, turning the issue into whether the arithmetic skeleton B_nat is already enough.

Bombieri presents the finite-field case as the strongest structural evidence for RH because the zeta function of a curve over F_q has an Euler product, functional equation, and a Zeta-function form whose zeros have absolute value q^(-1/2) in the RH case. He then broadens the picture to general varieties, where the characteristic roots, meaning the reciprocals of zeros and poles, are interpreted as Frobenius eigenvalues on etale cohomology.

The conceptual move is an analytic-to-geometric bridge. Classical zeta language is re-expressed through divisors, Frobenius, and cohomology, but the source is explicit that this remains evidence and analogy for the classical RH, not a mechanism that already proves the classical statement.

Conrey presents Weil's explicit formula as a prime-zero duality and then turns RH into a positivity test. For admissible h of the stated quadratic form, nonnegativity of the zero sum becomes equivalent to RH.

Li's sequence makes that positivity problem discrete: the lambda_n are given both by a zero sum and by derivatives of log xi(s) at s = 1. The span's real content is this reframing from geometry of zeros to positivity of a functional or sequence, while also acknowledging that the source does not yet explain why those quantities should be positive.

Problem E packages RH into the divisor-sum inequality sigma(n) <= H_n + exp(H_n) log(H_n), with equality only at n = 1, and Theorem 1.1 states that this problem is equivalent to RH. The unit also explains why the reformulation matters: it shifts the visible objects from zeta zeros to harmonic numbers and divisor sums.

But the source is equally explicit that the apparent elementary surface does not remove the underlying hardness. The equivalence runs through Robin's criterion and the deeper results behind it, so the mathematical operation is a representation change, not a simplification that dissolves the original difficulty.

interpretations.interpretation:
The unit states a sharp RH-conditional upper-bound theorem for zeta moments and then immediately rewrites the moment integral as an average of exp(2k log |zeta(1/2 + it)|). That identity is the conceptual hinge: the moment problem is recast as a question about the distribution of log |zeta| as t varies.

This is a genuine representation change, because the later heuristic discussion can then reason about how often log |zeta| takes given sizes instead of manipulating raw powers directly. I am not relying on the exact displayed logarithmic exponent in the theorem line, since that part of the OCR is locally ambiguous, only on the clearly readable theorem intent and exponential identity.

The span makes its own novelty explicit: it aims to count characters with the desired nonvanishing property directly, rather than reaching them through moments of L-functions. To do that it introduces a Barban-Vehov mollifier whose associated coefficients a(n) vanish on an initial range, and it studies one contour integral that can be expanded both as a Dirichlet sum and as L(s, chi)M(s, chi) plus a shifted integral.

That setup turns pointwise nonvanishing into a family-level counting mechanism. The fixed-point theorem and the interval theorem use the same device, but the excerpt also marks the boundary between them: for the interval result the choice of Y matters and is taken to be a power of q, whereas for the fixed-point result the source says the choice is much less delicate.

Starting from Sierra's Hamiltonian H_S=x(p+ell_p^2/p), the span writes the nonlinear Euler-Lagrange equation and identifies an eight-dimensional sl(3,R) Lie symmetry algebra for it. The authors then choose an abelian intransitive subalgebra, derive the point transformation (x,t)->(x~,t~), and use it to linearize the nonlinear equation to the free-particle equation.

The conceptual gain is not a slogan about symmetry but a concrete representation change that preserves the relevant structure. Once the free-particle form is exposed, a Lagrangian with five Noether symmetries is selected and quantization is carried out by preserving those symmetries, yielding the displayed Schroedinger equation. The span is therefore about symmetry-controlled linearization and quantization, not about any later zeta claim outside the excerpt.

The span builds a local transfer principle from zeta zeros to random matrices. It reviews the conjecture that scaled zeta zeros on the mean-spacing scale have the same local statistics as CUE eigenphases, cites Montgomery's restricted-range theorem and numerical evidence, and then says that locally determined zeta statistics high on the critical line may be modeled by the corresponding statistics of CUE characteristic polynomials.

That is a concrete model-transfer bridge, but it is explicitly local and heuristic. The support is short-range spectral agreement, not a theorem about all value statistics of zeta, so the modeling claim has to stay attached to the scale restriction and the conjectural status of the transfer.

The source treats zero-freeness near sigma = 1 as an exclusion problem driven by explicit size control on zeta(s). After surveying earlier regions, it singles out a Vinogradov-Korobov style upper bound as the input that supports the widest known log^(-2/3)(log log)^(-1/3) barrier shape.

The main theorem of the span is not a new qualitative shape but an explicit numerical version of that barrier: a zero too close to 1 would contradict the stated magnitude estimate. What survives cleanly here is the bridge from explicit growth bounds to a forbidden zero region, not the finer constants inside the supporting lemma.

The paper begins by saying that the zero theory of zeta^(alpha) is too weak to support a critical-line story for fractional derivatives. Rather than pretend otherwise, the span changes representation and asks what prime-information content survives in a half-plane where the manipulations are legal.

Theorem 4.3 answers that by linking zeta^(alpha)(s) for Re(s) < 0 to a prime-power double series, with the weak equivalence that the two sides converge or diverge together. The operative move is to trade an unavailable zero picture for an Euler-product-style prime expansion.

The source embeds the RH question into the one-parameter family H_t evolving under backward heat flow. Newman provides the threshold constant Lambda such that H_t has only real zeros exactly for t >= Lambda, so RH becomes the upper bound Lambda <= 0. The paper's result is the complementary lower bound Lambda >= 0, obtained by contradiction.

The conceptual gain is that zero location becomes a dynamical boundary problem. Assuming Lambda < 0 forces increasingly rigid local-equilibrium behavior for zeros of H_0, and the source says that this rigidity conflicts with known local zero statistics for zeta, such as Montgomery-type pair-correlation information.

This repaired unit introduces freedom into Levinson's method at two levels. The mollifier coefficient b(n, P) is defined using a polynomial P with endpoint conditions P(0) = 0 and P(1) = 1, and P is said to be optimizable by calculus of variations. At the same time, the auxiliary object is widened from zeta(s) + a(s) zeta'(s) to a general derivative combination sum_n a_n(s) zeta^(n)(s).

The proof burden is therefore relocated from zeta itself to a tunable surrogate. The source explicitly ties that surrogate to the payoff: if the chosen combination has few enough zeros to the right of the critical line, one gets a lower bound on the proportion of zeta zeros on the critical line.

interpretations.interpretation:
Assuming RH, the excerpt splits log|zeta(1/2+it)| into two pieces: a prime sum that still behaves like a truncated Euler product, and a nearby-zero correction. It then says the zero term is usually O(1), is sign-favorable for upper bounds, and leaves the main variance in the prime contribution.

The representation gain comes from splitting that prime contribution into short prime ranges. Later blocks contribute less variance, so the model is not one undifferentiated Dirichlet polynomial but a stack of correlated prime blocks that can be analyzed separately.

The source treats the Baez-Duarte sequence as a numerically visible wave dominated by the first zeta zero, and then asks what a failure of RH would have to look like in that representation. The author's claim is that hypothetical off-critical-line zeros would contribute terms so tiny, because of their expected huge imaginary parts, that any visible violation of the criterion would be pushed to astronomically large k.

This is explicitly speculative rather than established asymptotic control. The trustworthy content here is the scale-separation idea, the source's insistence that the plotted wave is governed by the first zero, and the open problem it states: relating the largest verified k-range to actual information about zeros on the critical line.

interpretations.interpretation:
The alternate proof of Li's theorem moves from coefficient positivity to eigenangle geometry. The resolvent on the unit circle is written in Fourier form, lambda_n is extracted from its imaginary part, and the Dyson-Schwinger relation in the unitary model then gives lambda_n as a sum of 1-cos(n theta_i).

Once that representation exists, positivity is immediate term by term. The proof is therefore a change of representation from Li numbers to a trigonometric sum over eigenangles.

Connes compares a semiclassical periodic-orbit expansion for the oscillatory counting term with the Euler-product expansion coming from zeta. Read as an analogy, that term-by-term matching proposes what a hypothetical Riemann flow would have to look like: primitive orbits indexed by primes, period log p, instability exponent +/- log p, and no time-reversal symmetry.

The important content is not a finished flow but the obstructions the comparison exposes. The overall sign is wrong, and the finite-repeat denominator matches only asymptotically rather than exactly, so the span functions as a constraint-and-failure analysis for any spectral-dynamical model.

The section treats a larger verified RH height as a reusable quantitative input rather than an isolated computational fact. Via Buthe's criterion, RH up to height H transfers directly to Schoenfeld-type bounds for psi, theta, and pi throughout a corresponding finite x-range.

The same transfer idea is then listed for zero-free regions, reciprocal-zeta bounds, zero-density estimates, and sign-change problems, with the authors explicitly warning that some improvements would be only slight. The unit's mechanism is therefore downstream conversion of finite certified zero verification into explicit inequalities.

The excerpt shifts the object of study from zeros of zeta to nonreal zeros of zeta^(k). Under RH it states aggregate asymptotics for the sum of beta^(k)-1/2 up to height T, a short-interval analogue of that sum, and the counting function N_k(T). It then introduces the normalizing functions F(s) and G_k(s) associated with the functional equation.

The concrete move is to study derivative zeros through aggregate displacement and counting statistics rather than through individual zero locations. In this span F and G_k function as setup and normalization, not yet as the displayed proof mechanism, so the trustworthy interpretation remains at the level of RH-conditional result formulation and the bookkeeping needed to transport functional-equation structure to zeta^(k).

Theorem 3 extracts an exact identity between sigma_k, eta_{k-1}, and zeta(k) by working inside one logarithmic expansion of xi(s). The proof first evaluates the zeta-value sum that appears after reordering a double series, then compares coefficients of powers of 1-s on both sides.

The value of the unit is that it aligns two coefficient languages in one representation. The eta-sequence and the zeta-value correction do not meet by external analogy; they are forced together by the same log xi expansion.

interpretations.interpretation:
The unit identifies a precise failure mode in the Nyman-Beurling program: the natural finite approximants F_n and the Selberg approximation may converge in weaker senses, yet finite-scale combinations are obstructed in the Hilbert space H by a lower bound that makes any such convergence extremely slow.

The repair is to stop truncating the scale parameter. The paper defines f_s(x)=sum mu(a)rho_a(x)/a^s over the full range of a, interprets it as a correction of 1/zeta(s), and then claims that under RH one has f_epsilon in B_nat while unconditionally f_epsilon tends to -chi in H as epsilon decreases to 0. The move is analytic weighting in place of finite cutoff.

The expansion starts by replacing a sharp cutoff with incomplete-gamma smoothing. Mellin inversion of Gamma(a,x) turns the smoothed Dirichlet series into a Perron-type integral, and contour shifts across z=0 and z=1-s generate explicit residue terms.

The resulting representation writes zeta(s) as a smoothed Dirichlet series plus correction terms whose coefficients A_m involve shifted zeta values. Exponential smoothing and residue calculus systematically unfold correction structure that a hard truncation would hide.

The source treats modularity as a machine that converts partition-function data into zero-indexed oscillation frequencies. Using the Rankin-Selberg-Zagier relation between a modular integral and constant-term asymptotics, it says that the difference between those quantities oscillates with frequencies universally determined by the nontrivial zeros of zeta.

The paper then states a conditional physical interpretation: for classically stable vacua, high-mass graded boson-fermion differences must follow a universal alternating pattern. Those claims are explicitly limited to the stable case and become heuristic once tachyon issues enter.
interpretations.unit_type: main claim linking stability and zeta zeros
interpretations.context_limit: The formal proof machinery comes later, but the claim itself is stated cleanly here.

interpretations.interpretation:
The theorem gives weighted and unweighted cubic-moment asymptotics with a degree-six polynomial in log x and a sharper error term, while also saying the weighted version shows the best error obtainable by the present method. The span then explains that the same multiple-Dirichlet-series framework should recover all coefficients of the main polynomial.

What remains tentative is also stated in the source. The authors expect an additional simple pole at w=3/4 for Z(1/2,1/2,1/2,w), but they do not claim it here as established fact. So the unit supports a bookkeeping role for the higher-dimensional series and an explicitly marked possible refinement, not a proven extra mechanism.

The source defines the one-level density D(F, phi) by scaling ordinates of zeros near 1/2 by log conductor, averaging that statistic over a family ordered by conductor, and comparing the result to explicit candidate densities for orthogonal and symplectic symmetry types. The theorem then states orthogonal limits for the listed GL2-related families under GRH and the support restriction on phi-hat.

The operation is to compress an entire family of zero sets into one observable that can be matched against a symmetry template. The boundary matters: conductor scaling and compact Fourier support are part of what the theorem actually controls, rather than incidental packaging.

The correlation statistic F(x,T) is broken into named pieces rather than treated as one opaque asymptotic. In the stated x-range, the theorem is rewritten as a signed sum of T1 through T7, and the source then evaluates those pieces using earlier lemmas and explicit integrals involving f.

That decomposition is analytic structure, not bookkeeping fluff. Different terms carry different logarithmic, constant, and integral contributions, so the pair-correlation quantity becomes interpretable source by source.

Corollary 3 shows that one quarter of the original interval still retains the full RH signal once the right correction terms are added. The centered sum up to 1/4 is rewritten in terms of odd-part quantities, and the resulting O(x^{1/2+epsilon}) condition is stated to be equivalent to RH.

The key move is congruence compression. By dividing the earlier object into residue classes mod 4, the source transports the full criterion into a thinner statistic without changing the logical content of the RH condition.

The computation is presented as a sign-certification method, not merely as large-scale evaluation of Z(t). The source fixes the Riemann-Siegel approximation, inserts Gabcke's remainder bound, and then carries out machine-level roundoff analysis for two implementations on a specified height range.

That error analysis is the mathematical core. Once safe upper bounds for the computed error are in place, sign determinations of the Hardy Z-function become rigorous witnesses, and the source reports that method B never failed to certify the sign in the investigated range.

Before the later zero-statistics argument, the paper engineers a cutoff with a flat interior, narrow support enlargement, and explicit derivative control. It starts from an indicator, repeatedly averages it over an interval of width Delta=(2^K U)^(-1), and thereby constructs Psi_U, which equals 1 on the central interval and has derivative bounds of order U^j.

The unit is about custom smoothing rather than generic mollification. Repeated averaging preserves the useful bulk of the cutoff while shaping it into an object whose analytic transforms can be handled later.

The theorem models truncated Euler products as functions on a torus of prime phases and then studies the induced value distributions. For log zeta_n and its derivative, the source obtains absolutely continuous distributions with densities F_n,a and G_n,a, and for a>1/2 it proves convergence to limiting densities with high regularity and positivity.

The threshold at a=1/2 is the real mechanism. Above it, the relevant series have convergent majorants and the density theory goes through; at a=1/2 that support disappears.

A mesoscopic fluctuation law for log zeta is transferred to zero counts through the counting formula N(t). The source states a Gaussian-process limit for a normalized field built from mesoscopic shifts of log zeta, describes it in Brownian-plus-disordered terms, and then derives central-limit statements for the number of zeros in intervals of length (log t)^delta and for the corresponding endpoint-indexed counting process.

The bridge is operational rather than rhetorical. Value fluctuations become zero-count fluctuations because Im log zeta enters the counting formula directly, and the unit explicitly keeps this mesoscopic phenomenon distinct from microscopic pair-correlation laws.

This exact unit is background, but it still performs a concrete bridge. It locates the nontrivial zeros in the critical strip, states the symmetry about the critical line and real axis, recalls RH, and records that the prime number theorem is equivalent to the absence of zeros on the boundary line Re(s)=1.

The mathematical move here is not the later physics story but the prime-zero interface itself. Prime distribution is introduced through the opening of Riemann's explicit formula, and the prime number theorem is recast as a boundary-zero statement for zeta.
interpretations.context_limit: The modular-function machinery producing the claim is developed later, but the statement here is self-contained at the level of mechanism.

interpretations.interpretation:
The contour is deformed around zeros on the critical line, and the proof studies the sign of Re(F'/F) on the resulting boundary. If there is a monotone sequence of heights where that real part stays negative on the top edges, then the change of argument of F'/F is controlled and the zero counts of F and F' stay locked together. If not, repeated sign failure forces zeros with 1-sigma_0<beta<1/2 to occur frequently enough to produce the needed lower bound.

The sign of the logarithmic derivative is the control variable. The same quantity can either certify count equality or, when the sign certificate fails, generate the bad zeros required by the theorem.

The theorem states a one-level density formula for quadratic Dirichlet L-functions under the Ratios Conjecture and then compares it with the scaling-limit density for USp(2N). The source keeps the arithmetic lower-order terms visible while also exhibiting the universal symplectic main term.

The unit's real move is separation of levels. Averaged low-lying zeros are represented by a test-function integral whose leading behavior matches the symplectic kernel, while the detailed gamma, zeta, and arithmetic factors account for finite-level corrections. The simplest reduction to -g(0)/2 is explicitly restricted to compact Fourier support.

Assuming RH, Proposition 3.1 expresses the zero-counting function N_k(T) in terms of the main T log T term plus the arguments of G_k(1/2+iT) and zeta(1/2+iT). The proof compares contour formulas at b and b0=1/2-2 delta, decomposes the difference into J1 through J15, imports earlier estimates for some pieces, and uses holomorphic logarithmic branches with Cauchy's theorem to show that J13 and J15 are O_k(delta). Letting delta go to zero collapses the remaining strip integrals to critical-line endpoint arguments.

The mechanism is endpoint extraction. A strip-level argument-counting identity is reduced to boundary data on the critical line by proving that the non-endpoint corrections wash out in the delta -> 0 limit.

The Wigner matrix of the Riemann-Siegel state is split into diagonal pieces and off-diagonal interference pieces. For tau=0 the truncated state develops a wedge along the x-axis, while for tau>0 the diagonal Wigner functions rotate in phase space but the off-diagonal term only acquires time-dependent scaling phases and preserves its k-symmetry.

The source is not merely giving one formula for one state. It separates two dynamical roles inside the phase-space representation: rotating diagonal mass versus nonrotating interference structure.

The large-value problem is split into two explicit prime sums. After choosing A, x, and z from V and T, the source bounds log absolute zeta(1/2+it) by S1(t)+S2(t) plus a controlled V-term, so any t in the exceptional set must force either S2(t) to be large or S1(t) to exceed a slightly smaller threshold.

That dichotomy is the whole mechanism. Once the pointwise problem is replaced by two failure modes at different prime scales, separate moment estimates can bound the measure of each mode.

The overview starts from the counterfactual hypothesis Lambda<0 and says the paper no longer pursues only improved Lehmer-pair bounds. The proof strategy makes that claim quantitative by combining interval zero-counting formulas for H_t, the ODE evolution of zeros under backward heat flow, and Hamiltonian and energy functionals with monotonicity properties. After truncation and averaging, those controls force near-equilibrium behavior at t=0, and the source says that this prediction is then contradicted by known local zero statistics such as Montgomery pair correlation. Summing those interval inequalities and substituting earlier asymptotic formulas turns the spacing problem into an inequality among the constants a(k), b(k), and c(k). The resulting lower bound on normalized gaps is therefore obtained by bridging local interval geometry to global moment data, all under RH and the previously quoted asymptotics.

In the second phase of the algorithm, the quadratic-sums procedure is applied to F(K; a0-alpha0 x, b0), and the smallness of alpha0 means the effective length depends only weakly on x. Each iteration multiplies alpha0 upward and shortens the quadratic sum, until alpha0 nears 1 and the direct use of the same algorithm becomes awkward. The algorithmic move is deliberate type conversion. A long quadratic-sum problem is repeatedly traded for shorter but structurally richer sums, and once those higher-degree sums appear, dyadic subdivision and FFT precomputation take over as the efficient representation.

The span explains why RH-sensitive behavior for the divisor-sum inequality should be sought on a thin structured set rather than across all integers uniformly. Even if RH were false, the source says the resulting counterexamples should still be very sparse and very large.

The excerpt compares several inversion procedures applied to the same zeta-zero spectrum and says they produce the same potential, with inverse scattering giving uniqueness in one dimension. That removes the reconstruction method itself as the explanation for the observed fractal behavior.

The useful move is a robustness test under representation change. Riemann turns the Euler product into a weighted prime-power counting object and recovers it by Mellin-style inversion of log zeta. Bombieri recasts the same bridge as Weil's explicit formula, where one test function is read simultaneously on the zero side and the prime-power side, and in the function-field case as a Frobenius trace formula. AIM then uses that fixed dictionary to list prime-counting error terms and zero-location statements as equivalent formulations of the Riemann Hypothesis.

Bombieri's geometric trace reading is exact only in the function-field analogue, and AIM's unit is an overview map rather than a new proof route.

Lagarias turns the Riemann Hypothesis into an elementary-looking divisor-sum inequality while stating that the hard work is still carried by Robin's deeper criterion. Baez-Duarte sharpens Nyman-Beurling by asking for the same closure statement inside the thinner natural-number subfamily B_nat, so zero-location language becomes a Hilbert-space approximation problem without losing the global burden. Conrey then rewrites Weil's explicit formula as positivity, first for an admissible functional and then for Li's discrete sequence, while saying openly that the source still lacks a natural explanation for that positivity.

Limits: These are relocations of difficulty, not easier proofs. The Lagarias and Baez-Duarte criteria remain all-n or full-closure statements, and Conrey's unit is explicit that the positivity formulation still has an interpretive gap.

Montgomery studies zero spacings through a Fourier/form-factor observable and proves the random-matrix-looking behavior only on the restricted range below the frequency break. His conjectural continuation and Dyson's comparison then pick the unitary/Hermitian symmetry class and exclude neighboring real-symmetric and symplectic alternatives. Keating and Snaith extend that local transfer to zeta values by matching the mean-spacing scale with matrix size and then splitting the finite-height story into a universal CUE term plus a separate arithmetic correction built from primes.

Limits: The common structure is local statistical transfer, not an exact identification of zeta with a matrix model. Montgomery's theorem is range-limited, and Keating-Snaith explicitly keep finite-height arithmetic corrections separate from the universal random-matrix term.

Platt and Trudgian make explicit what that older span does not supply: sign changes on the critical line must be paired with a Turing-method zero count and rigorous numerical error control to certify that every expected zero in a finite height range has been found. Their second unit then shows what such finite certification can legitimately propagate to explicit bounds, while also marking which advertised gains are only slight or future.

Limits: The shared structure is the boundary between local detection and exhaustive accounting, not a general claim that computation proves RH. Lehmer's unit is exploratory local diagnosis without an explicit completeness theorem, and even the modern verified result remains finite-height evidence with bounded downstream reach.

Their CA-to-XA transfer step adds the missing transport rule: once an extremely abundant witness appears between consecutive colossally abundant numbers, the upper endpoint is forced into the witness class as well. Montgomery's heuristic continuation of the form factor beyond the proved small-alpha range turns zero spacing into a conjectural pair-correlation law. Mueller then uses averaged positivity rather than pointwise control: after weighting over shifts, one concrete shift survives, and that surviving positivity is converted into the existence of nearby primes. Goldston and Montgomery refine the same channel by splitting the correlation statistic into named terms whose different logarithmic and integral contributions can be tracked separately, making the prime-side transfer sensitive to more than one bulk asymptotic. The shared role is downstream transport from zero statistics to prime-pattern evidence.

Michel and VanderKam show two versions of family-level extraction for Dirichlet characters. At a fixed point, a mollified first moment and controlled second moment force a positive proportion of characters to satisfy L(a,chi) != 0; on a whole interval, short interval covering and Cauchy-integral localization convert the existence of a real zero into an averaged contour count, yielding a positive proportion with no real zero in the stated strip. Perelli and Pomykała use the same supply-versus-obstruction logic for quadratic twists of an elliptic curve, but with a different output variable: moment information creates a supply of useful twists, zero-density estimates limit how many can be spoiled by bad zero configurations, and Weil's explicit formula rewrites the remaining average-rank burden as the arithmetic correction term S(lambda,d). The shared role is not blanket nonvanishing. It is extraction of many good family members by comparing total supply against averaged obstructions rather than solving any individual L-function outright.

Limits: The conclusions are family-level and not constructive. Michel-VanderKam's slices give fixed-point nonvanishing and absence of real zeros on a segment for positive proportions of characters, while Perelli-Pomykala's slices concern average-rank and zero-density extraction for elliptic twists rather than a second direct nonvanishing theorem. All four units depend on averaged inputs, and the elliptic-twist side still needs explicit-formula and density control to manage the bad set.

Baez-Duarte shows why natural finite approximants fail in the needed Hilbert norm and repairs the route by replacing finite cutoff with analytic weighting across the full range of scales. Beltraminelli, Merlini, and Vega then make the same criterion family computationally legible by expanding R(x) and c_k in zero sums whose first mode dominates the visible wave, and by showing that alternating or Abel-type weighting converges where raw summation does not. Wolf sharpens the interpretive split by separating a smooth k^-2 trend from the genuinely interesting zero-indexed oscillation. The common role is not another equivalence statement but a stabilization-and-frequency decomposition of a fragile criterion.

Conrey and Keating then show, from the ascending coefficient side, that the diagonal part of a zeta moment matches the same zeta-factor object that appears in the swap recipe. In the later Type II analysis, near multiplicative equalities are turned into small additive defects via Farey-style parameters, and the apparent overcounting is finally reinterpreted as genuine automorphism multiplicity rather than an error. The shared role is structural unpacking of moments into a quotientable combinatorial geometry.

Limits: These units supply architecture, not final moment asymptotics on their own. Continuation, swap matching, and automorphism correction still leave hard off-diagonal estimation and convergence issues to later work.
